newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish mkt shrugs off budget, focus international.
newsitem.headline: Irish mkt shrugs off budget, focus international.

text.p: Irish financial markets shrugged off finance minister Ruairi Quinn's 1997 budget on Thursday, focusing instead on international developments, particularly a big overnight drop in sterling, traders said.
Quinn announced tax and spending increases of nearly 650 million punts in his annual budget on Wednesday, delivering the biggest tax reduction package in the history of the state.
But dealers said the budget had been well leaked and contained few surprises and developments overseas, especially sterling's performance, were as important for Irish inflation and interest rates.

Sterling fell by nearly six pfennigs overnight, dragging the Irish pound in its wake. The punt plunged by three pfennigs against the mark, falling to 2.6180 marks and dipping back below $1.60 to trade at $1.5990 by 0918 GMT.
Dealers said the Irish bond market was keeping a wary eye on currency developments as well as absorbing Quinn's budget.
Bonds were slightly lower in morning trade on Thursday but dealers said the market was trading in line with international markets and there was no evidence of any unilateral underperformance.
By 0920 GMT, five-year paper was 10 pence lower at 102.85, yielding 5.79 while 10-paper slipped 25 pence to 110.00, a yield of 6.55 percent.
Analysts agreed that Quinn's budget, possibly the last before the next Irish election, was stimulatory but views were mixed on whether it would have negative consequences for Irish inflation.

"The budget is going to add to growth. It's clearly very expansionary and very pro-cyclical and that is not the ideal policy to have at the moment so at the margin, we would expect the market to have a negative bias because of the budget," Padhraic Garvey, economist at Riada Stockbrokers told Reuters.
But NCB Stockbrokers said it did not believe the budget stimulus would have any significant adverse inflationary or balance of payments consequences.

"The GDP/GNP growth rates we and the Department of Finance forecast are, we believe, within the underlying potential of an economy that is benefiting from significantly positive structural influences right now," economist Dermot O'Brien said.
Others said the impact on bonds would be broadly neutral as European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would remain the driving force behind the Irish market.
"Ultimately, the direction of the market this year will depend on EMU developments," Bloxham economist Alan McQuaid said.
He noted, however, that the government had missed an opportunity to reduce Ireland's debt burden.
"There is no reason whatsoever why pursuit of a balanced budget should not be a legitimate and realistic objective in the Irish context," McQuaid said.
Quinn set a 1997 Exchequer borrowing target of 637 million punts or 1.6 percent of GNP, lower than many in the market had expected.
Measured for EMU purposes, the general government deficit is targeted at 1.5 percent of GDP. This is well below the Maastricht requirement of three percent and pleased the market, analysts said.
